newsitem.title: USA: US Surface Trans Board supports rail negotiations.
newsitem.headline: US Surface Trans Board supports rail negotiations.

text.p: Linda Morgan, chairman of U.S. Surface Transportation Board, reaffirmed Friday the board's support of private sector negotiations to resolve competitive-access issues in railroad mergers.

"What history has shown us is that private sector negotiations do result in the benefit to the parties involved and the public at large," Morgan said in a speech at National Mining Association's annual transportation conference.
Surface Transportation Board, commonly called the Surf Board, is the regulatory body responsible for overseeing U.S. railroads.

Morgan's remarks, coming the same day that executives in the takeover for Conrail are meeting to try to resolve their impasse, underscored comments she made recently encouraging rival bidders to negotiate.
Industry officials have credited her public comments for pushing CSX Corp and Norfolk Southern Corp into discussion.
The two railroads have been involved in a bitter four-month fight to acquire Conrail, the dominant railroad in the U.S. Northeast.
In October, Conrail's board agreed to be acquired by CSX in a cash and stock deal. Norfolk Southern followed up a week later with a hostile all-cash bid for Conrail.

While avoiding discussing the specifics of the Conrail case, Morgan said the board would continue to look to preserve competition in the nations rail network, as it had in the Union Pacific-Southern Pacific merger last year.

"When I look at the UP-SP decision, we were able to maintain the benefits associated with that merger and at the same time we were able to address the issues that dealt with competitive harmm", she said.

Separately, Morgan said the Surf Board had extended to one year the procedural schedule for filings in the Conrail case. The board had previously set a 300 day schedule, but Morgan cautioned that the board reserved the right to revise the schedule at any time.

Morgan was speaking to coal and utility industry representatives. Coal is one of the major commodities carried by U.S. freight railroads, accounting for 40 percent of the railroads' gross tonnage and about 20 pct of their revenues.
